1.text: COUNCIL OF THE FAMILY-GROUP. — I was told that in olden times, when

2.text: some awkward case in law (akauˊka-vaˊɪrg̣ɪn, “inconvenient substances,” the

3.text: usual Chukchee expression for trouble, trespass, crime¹) happened within the

4.text: limits of a family-group, the old men and the young men would hold a council.

5.text: The old men would sit down and talk about the case. The young men would

6.text: stand behind and listen. Likewise, when any trouble arose between two dif-

7.text: ferent family-groups, men from both sides would assemble. The old men of

8.text: each side would elect one or two speakers, who had to speak in turn, one

9.text: side after the other. The old men spoke “for the softness” (am-yêrkêˊtɪ), and

10.text: the younger men had to obey their decision. If, however, an agreement could

11.text: not be reached, or the parties particularly interested in the case refused to

12.text: listen to reason, the old men would say, “Let them [have a little] play”

13.text: (nuučveˊerkɪnet).² Then the interested parties, armed with spears, would have

14.text: an encounter. Of course, even such a duel would have been better than the

15.text: unorganized bloodshed of vendetta; but I am unable to say how far the above

16.text: description of the council corresponded to actual life; at least, in the modern

17.text: life of the Chukchee tribe, I do not know of anything similar to such councils

19.text: I mentioned previously that the Chukchee are eloquent in their own way;

20.text: so that, when anything happens, at the next gathering of the people — for

21.text: instance, during some ceremonial or on the occasion of a reindeer-race — it

22.text: is much talked about; and in this discussion, as is the custom, only the older

23.text: and more esteemed people take an important part. From this to a regular

24.text: council, however, is a long way. I mentioned in the chapter on marriage a

25.text: similar assertion by D. J. Melikoff,³ concerning the “council of elders.” This

26.text: assertion even pretended to refer to modern times. I expressed then also

27.text: my opinion that in modern times, so far as I know, no such councils are held

28.text: among the Chukchee. The law is regulated by personal action, and no public

29.text: institutions have anything to do with the judgment or punishment of the crime.

30.text: MURDER AND BLOOD-REVENGE WITHIN THE FAMILY-GROUP. — The principal

31.text: ¹ The Chukchee have no other general term covering the concept “crime.” Two roots, taiñ and qäs˙m,

32.text: several derivations of which are used in reference to crime, express only a trespass against religious prescriptions,

33.text: mostly of ceremonial character, and the “bad luck” which is the result thereof. Thus the adjective nɪtaˊɪnqên

34.text: means “bringing bad luck.” The opposite of it is nɪkɪˊntaqên (“bringing good luck,” “favorable”). The noun

35.text: taiˊñɪkut (pl.) with the meaning of “misfortune-protectors,” is used as a designation for charm-strings (cf. p. 353).

36.text: The noun qas˙muˊurg̣ɪn means “bad luck” coming from the influence of keˊlet, etc.

37.text: ² F. Boas mentions that among the Central Eskimo there exists a kind of temporary chief, who may give

38.text: orders, but that there is not the slightest obligation to obey his orders (Central Eskimo, p. 581). In the same

39.text: way among the Chukchee the advice of the old men was not binding upon the interested parties.
